params.question: A child frequently makes careless errors in schoolwork, appears not to listen when spoken to directly, and struggles to organise daily tasks. According to the ICD-11/DSM-5 classification of ADHD, which symptom domain do these features belong to?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction are a defining feature of Autism Spectrum Disorder, not ADHD. ADHD is classified into inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity domains.

Hyperactivity-impulsivity features include fidgeting, leaving the seat, running or climbing inappropriately, and difficulty waiting turns — these are motor and impulse-control symptoms, not attentional ones.

Correct. Careless mistakes, poor sustained attention, seeming not to listen, and difficulty organising tasks are hallmark features of the inattention domain of ADHD as classified in both ICD-11 and DSM-5.
Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities are part of the diagnostic criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder, not ADHD.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two core symptom domains of ADHD: inattention (poor focus, careless errors, disorganisation) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (fidgeting, interrupting, difficulty waiting). These are distinct from ASD features.

Well done. Recognising which symptom domain a clinical feature belongs to is essential for accurate subtyping of ADHD — predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined presentation.

params.question: Why does mild intellectual disability — which accounts for approximately 85% of all cases of IDD — typically come to clinical attention only at school age?

answers.text: Because standardised IQ tests cannot be reliably administered before age 6

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Developmental screening instruments and clinical assessments can be used well before school age. The delay in recognition relates to the subtlety of the cognitive deficit, not to testing limitations.

answers.text: Because mild ID is always caused by a chromosomal abnormality that is detectable only by karyotyping at age 5

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Most cases of mild intellectual disability have no identifiable chromosomal abnormality. The aetiology is often multifactorial, and the delay in diagnosis relates to the child's adequate early social development, not to the timing of genetic testing.

answers.text: Because parents typically do not seek medical attention until the child is enrolled in school

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While parental concern plays a role, the primary reason is that children with mild ID develop social and communication skills adequately during the pre-school years — their limitations are only unmasked by formal academic demands.

answers.text: Because pre-school development appears only mildly delayed, and academic demands at school first exceed the child's cognitive capacity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In mild ID, social and communication skills develop adequately in the pre-school years. It is only when formal academic demands are introduced that the gap between the child's capacity and age-appropriate expectations becomes apparent.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is that children with mild ID develop social and communication skills reasonably well in early childhood — it is the academic demands of formal schooling that first unmask their cognitive limitations.
Exactly. Understanding why mild ID 'hides in plain sight' during pre-school years helps clinicians counsel parents and advocate for early developmental screening.

interactions.label: A 9-year-old boy's teacher reports significant hyperactivity and poor attention

params.question: A 9-year-old boy's teacher reports significant hyperactivity and poor attention in class. His parents request a definitive test to confirm ADHD. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

answers.text: Order a CT scan of the brain to visualise prefrontal cortical abnormalities

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no brain scan that can establish a diagnosis of ADHD. Neuroimaging findings such as reduced prefrontal volume are research-level observations, not diagnostic tools in clinical practice.

answers.text: Gather a detailed developmental history, caregiver and teacher reports, and conduct direct clinical observation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ADHD diagnosis rests on a multi-informant, multi-method assessment. The developmental history is the cornerstone — confirming symptom onset before age 12 (DSM-5), duration of at least 6 months, multi-setting presence, and functional impairment.

answers.text: Administer a single standardised rating scale and base the diagnosis on its score alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While standardised rating scales (such as the Conners or Vanderbilt scales) are useful adjuncts, no single scale can establish the diagnosis. ADHD diagnosis requires integration of developmental history, multi-informant reports, and clinical observation.

answers.text: Prescribe a therapeutic trial of methylphenidate and diagnose ADHD if behaviour improves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A medication trial is not a diagnostic strategy. Stimulant response is not specific to ADHD — improved attention with methylphenidate can occur regardless of diagnosis. A thorough diagnostic assessment must precede any treatment decision.

overallFeedback.feedback: The diagnostic assessment for ADHD integrates developmental history (onset before age 12, at least 6 months duration, multi-setting impairment), caregiver and teacher reports, clinical observation, and standardised instruments — not any single investigation.

Correct. Remember: there is no blood test, brain scan, or single rating scale that establishes an ADHD or ASD diagnosis — a multi-informant, multi-method assessment integrating developmental history, clinical observation, and collateral reports is the standard of care.
